messages.content: explain the french revolution
The French Revolution (1789-1799) was a period of radical political and societal change in France. What aspect interests you most - the causes, key events, or its impact?
what caused it
what is the theme of to kill a mockingbird
idk shakespeare's macbeth

Macbeth is a tragedy about ambition, guilt, and the corrupting nature of power. The play follows Macbeth, a Scottish general, who receives a prophecy that he will become king. What would you like to explore first?
why does macbeth kill duncan

Macbeth kills King Duncan due to a combination of factors:
  • The witches' prophecy plants the seed of ambition
  • Lady Macbeth pressures and manipulates him
  • His own ambition drives him
Do you think he would have done it without Lady Macbeth's influence?
probably not, she seems really manipulative

That's a great observation! Lady Macbeth does use powerful manipulation tactics - she questions his manhood and courage. However, some argue Macbeth already had the ambition within him. What evidence from the play supports your view?
well he seemed hesitant at first and kept having second thoughts
what was the renaissance

The Renaissance was a cultural movement spanning roughly the 14th to 17th centuries, beginning in Italy. It marked a 'rebirth' of interest in classical Greek and Roman culture, art, and learning. Would you like to focus on the art, science, or philosophy of this period?
tell me about the art
what's existentialism
i need help with my essay on the great gatsby
I'd be happy to help! What's your essay topic or prompt?
i have to analyze the symbolism of the green light

The green light is one of the most important symbols in the novel. It appears at the end of Daisy's dock and represents Gatsby's hopes and dreams. What do you think it symbolizes beyond just Daisy herself?
maybe the american dream?

Exactly! The green light represents the American Dream - the idea that anyone can achieve success and happiness through hard work. But think about this: does Gatsby ever actually reach the green light? What might Fitzgerald be saying about the American Dream?
that its unattainable?
explain world war 1

World War I (1914-1918) was a global conflict primarily centered in Europe. It's often called 'The Great War.' The main causes are summarized by the acronym MAIN:
  • Militarism
  • Alliances
  • Imperialism
  • Nationalism
What would you like to understand better?
what started it exactly
who was socrates

Socrates (470-399 BCE) was an ancient Greek philosopher considered one of the founders of Western philosophy. He's famous for his method of questioning, called the Socratic method, and for saying 'I know that I know nothing.' What draws your interest to him?
why was he executed

Socrates was tried and executed in Athens on charges of 'corrupting the youth' and 'impiety' (not believing in the city's gods). He was sentenced to death by drinking hemlock. Many historians believe the real reason was political - his questioning challenged Athenian democracy and he had connections to controversial figures. Do you think his execution was justified?
no that seems unfair just for asking questions
what is the cold war
can you help me understand 1984 by orwell

1984 is a dystopian novel about a totalitarian society ruled by 'Big Brother.' It explores themes of surveillance, propaganda, and the manipulation of truth. Have you started reading it, or do you need an overview first?
i finished it but i dont get what doublethink means

Doublethink is the ability to hold two contradictory beliefs simultaneously and accept both as true. For example, the Party's slogans 'War is Peace' and 'Freedom is Slavery' require doublethink. It's a form of psychological manipulation that allows the Party to control reality. Can you think of any real-world examples of doublethink?
like when politicians say one thing but do another and people just accept it?
what caused the civil rights movement

The Civil Rights Movement emerged from centuries of racial injustice in America, but key catalysts in the 1950s-60s included:
  • Segregation laws (Jim Crow)
  • The murder of Emmett Till
  • Rosa Parks' arrest
  • The Brown v. Board of Education decision
Which aspect would you like to explore further?
tell me more about rosa parks
what is the meaning of life according to philosophy
explain the odyssey

The Odyssey is an ancient Greek epic poem by Homer, telling the story of Odysseus's 10-year journey home after the Trojan War. It explores themes of homecoming, loyalty, cunning, and the hero's journey. Are you reading it for class?
yes and i dont understand why it takes him so long to get home

Great question! Odysseus faces many obstacles:
  • He angers Poseidon by blinding his son the Cyclops
  • Encounters the witch Circe
  • Navigates past the Sirens
  • And more...
But beyond physical obstacles, his journey is also about personal growth and proving his worth. What obstacles have you read about so far?
the cyclops part, that was intense

The Cyclops episode is one of the most famous! Odysseus shows his cleverness by calling himself 'Nobody' so when Polyphemus cries for help, he says 'Nobody is hurting me.' But Odysseus also shows his fatal flaw - hubris (excessive pride) - when he reveals his real name as he escapes. Why do you think he did that?
i guess he wanted credit for outsmarting the cyclops
what was the industrial revolution

The Industrial Revolution (roughly 1760-1840) was a period of major technological, economic, and social change. It began in Britain with the shift from hand production to machine manufacturing. Would you like to learn about its causes, effects, or key inventions?
how did it affect regular people
what is romanticism in literature
help me analyze a poem
I'd be happy to help! Which poem are you analyzing?
the road not taken by robert frost

Great choice! This poem is often misunderstood. Many people think it's about taking the unconventional path, but Frost actually describes the two roads as 'really about the same.' What do you think the poem is really saying?
wait so its not about being different?

It's more nuanced! The speaker admits the paths were 'worn really about the same.' The key is in the last stanza - 'I shall be telling this with a sigh / Somewhere ages and ages hence.' Frost may be commenting on how we create narratives about our choices after the fact, making them seem more significant than they were. Does that change how you see the poem?
yeah thats kind of mind blowing actually
explain the difference between sunni and shia islam
what was the harlem renaissance

The Harlem Renaissance (1920s-1930s) was a cultural, artistic, and intellectual movement centered in the Harlem neighborhood of New York City. It celebrated African American culture and produced influential literature, music, and art. Are you interested in the literature, music, or visual arts of this period?
the literature please

Key literary figures include:
  • Langston Hughes
  • Zora Neale Hurston
  • Claude McKay
  • Countee Cullen
Their work explored themes of racial identity, the African American experience, and the 'double consciousness' of being Black in America. Have you read any works from this period?
we're reading their eyes were watching god
why did rome fall

The fall of the Western Roman Empire in 476 CE resulted from multiple factors:
  • Economic troubles
  • Military overextension
  • Political corruption
  • Invasions by Germanic tribes
  • Possibly even lead poisoning
Historians still debate which factors were most important. Which theory interests you most?
the barbarian invasions
what is utilitarianism

Utilitarianism is an ethical theory that says the best action is the one that maximizes overall happiness or 'utility.' It was developed by philosophers Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill. The famous principle is 'the greatest good for the greatest number.' Does this make sense so far?
yes but what if making most people happy hurts some people

You've identified the main criticism of utilitarianism! This is called the 'tyranny of the majority' problem. For example, if torturing one innocent person could make 1000 people happy, would that be moral? Most people say no, which suggests there might be some rights that shouldn't be violated regardless of the outcome. What do you think?
that seems wrong, some things should just never be done
how do i improve my sat reading score

Great question! The SAT Reading section tests comprehension, evidence-based reasoning, and vocabulary in context. Key strategies include:
  • Reading the questions first
  • Focusing on main ideas
  • Practicing with timed passages
What area are you struggling with most?
i run out of time
what's the difference between a primary and secondary source
i dont understand subject verb agreement

Subject-verb agreement means the subject and verb in a sentence must match in number. A singular subject needs a singular verb, and a plural subject needs a plural verb. For example:
  • 'The dog runs' (singular)
  • 'The dogs run' (plural)
What's confusing you about it?
when there's words between the subject and verb

That's a common trick on the SAT! The key is to identify the true subject and ignore interrupting phrases. For example: 'The box of chocolates IS on the table' - 'box' is singular, not 'chocolates.' Try this one: 'The students in the class (is/are) excited.' Which is correct?
are, because students is plural
how do i analyze a historical document

When analyzing a historical document, consider:
  • Who wrote it?
  • When and where?
  • What was the purpose?
  • Who was the audience?
  • What biases might exist?
This is often called 'sourcing.' Would you like to practice with a specific document?
yeah can we do the declaration of independence
when do i use a semicolon
i keep getting inference questions wrong on sat reading

Inference questions ask you to draw conclusions based on evidence in the passage. The key is that the answer must be directly supported by the text - don't make assumptions beyond what's written. What kind of inferences are tripping you up?
i always pick answers that seem right but are too extreme

That's a really common issue! SAT answers are usually moderate and well-supported. Watch out for words like 'always,' 'never,' 'all,' or 'none' - these extreme answers are usually wrong. The correct answer is typically more nuanced. Want to try a practice question?
yes please
what is bias in a source

Bias is when a source presents information from a particular perspective or with a certain agenda. Every source has some bias based on the author's background, purpose, and audience. Recognizing bias helps you evaluate how reliable and objective a source is. Can you think of examples where bias might appear?
like if a company writes about their own product
whats the difference between who and whom

'Who' is used for subjects (the one doing the action), and 'whom' is used for objects (the one receiving the action). A trick: if you can replace it with 'he/she,' use 'who.' If you can replace it with 'him/her,' use 'whom.' For example:
  • 'Who called?' (He called)
  • 'Whom did you call?' (I called him)
Make sense?
oh thats actually a really helpful trick
how do i identify the authors tone
can you explain parallelism

Parallelism means using the same grammatical structure for similar ideas in a sentence. For example:
  • ✓ 'She likes swimming, running, and biking' (all -ing verbs)
  • ✗ 'She likes swimming, to run, and bikes'
The SAT frequently tests this. Want to see some examples?
yes that would help

Here's a practice question: Which is correct?

A) 'The job requires typing, filing, and to answer phones.'
B) 'The job requires typing, filing, and answering phones.'

Think about what structure is being repeated.
B because theyre all ing words
how do i evaluate if a source is credible

To evaluate credibility, use the CRAAP test:
  • Currency (is it recent?)
  • Relevance (does it fit your needs?)
  • Authority (who wrote it?)
  • Accuracy (is it supported by evidence?)
  • Purpose (why was it written?)
Which of these do you find hardest to assess?
authority i think, how do i know if someone is an expert
i dont get dangling modifiers

A dangling modifier is a phrase that doesn't clearly connect to what it's supposed to modify. For example:
  • ✗ 'Walking to school, the rain started.' (This implies the rain was walking!)
  • ✓ 'Walking to school, I got caught in the rain.'
The modifier must be next to what it describes. See how that works?
oh so whatever comes right after the comma should be doing the action
how do i find the main idea of a passage
what are rhetorical devices

Rhetorical devices are techniques writers use to persuade or create an effect. Common ones include:
  • Metaphor
  • Repetition
  • Rhetorical questions
  • Parallelism
  • Appeals to emotion (pathos), logic (logos), or credibility (ethos)
Are you analyzing a speech or essay?
yeah we have to analyze mlks i have a dream speech

Perfect example! That speech is full of rhetorical devices. The repetition of 'I have a dream' creates rhythm and emphasis. He uses metaphors like 'the bank of justice' and appeals to both American ideals and religious imagery. What devices have you noticed so far?
the repetition for sure and lots of imagery
when do i use commas with however

It depends on how 'however' is used!
  • If it starts a new independent clause, use a semicolon before and comma after: 'I studied; however, I failed.'
  • If it's an interrupter mid-sentence, use commas on both sides: 'The test, however, was harder than expected.'
  • If it means 'in whatever way,' no commas: 'However you solve it is fine.'
Which usage are you seeing?
the first one mostly, connecting two sentences
how do i answer evidence based questions on the sat
what is corroboration in history

Corroboration means checking if multiple sources agree on the same information. If several independent sources say the same thing, the information is more likely to be accurate. It's like being a detective - you want multiple witnesses! Why do you think historians use this technique?
because one source could be wrong or biased
i keep mixing up its and it's

'It's' with an apostrophe is a contraction meaning 'it is' or 'it has.' 'Its' without an apostrophe is possessive, like 'his' or 'her.' Test it by expanding:
  • 'It's raining' = 'It is raining' ✓
  • 'The dog wagged its tail' - you wouldn't say 'it is tail'
Make sense?
so the apostrophe doesnt mean possessive here

Exactly! That's the tricky part. With 'its,' the apostrophe ONLY means contraction, never possession. It's an exception because 'its' is a pronoun like 'his' or 'hers' - none of those have apostrophes for possession either. Want to try some practice sentences?
sure that would help
how do i compare two passages on the sat

For paired passages, first read each one separately and understand its main argument. Then look for:
  • Where they agree
  • Where they disagree
  • How they would respond to each other
  • What evidence each uses
The questions often ask how Author 1 would respond to Author 2's claims. What's challenging you about these?
keeping track of both arguments at once
what is contextualization in history
explain comma splices

A comma splice is when you incorrectly join two independent clauses with just a comma. For example: 'I went to the store, I bought milk.' Both parts could stand alone as sentences, so a comma isn't enough. You can fix it with:
  • A period
  • A semicolon
  • Adding a conjunction like 'and'
Got it?
so i need more than just a comma between two complete sentences
how do i identify the authors purpose

Author's purpose is WHY they wrote something. The main purposes are:
  • To inform (give facts)
  • To persuade (convince you of something)
  • To entertain (engage or amuse)
  • To explain (teach how something works)
Look at the tone, word choice, and what the author wants you to think or do after reading. What kind of passage are you working with?
a science article about climate change

Science articles can be tricky because they might inform AND persuade. Look for clues:
  • Does it just present data objectively?
  • Or does it use words like 'must,' 'should,' or 'urgent' that suggest the author wants action?
  • Is there a call to action at the end?
it does say we need to act now so probably persuade
what are transition words and why do they matter
how do i analyze political cartoons

Political cartoons use visual elements to make arguments. Look for:
  • Symbols (what do objects represent?)
  • Caricature (exaggerated features)
  • Labels (text that identifies things)
  • Irony or satire
  • The overall message
Also consider when it was created and what events it's responding to. Do you have a specific cartoon to analyze?
its one about the gilded age with a fat guy on a money bag

That sounds like a classic critique of wealthy industrialists or 'robber barons.' The fat figure likely represents greed or excess wealth, and the money bag symbolizes their enormous fortunes. These cartoons often criticized the gap between rich and poor during that era. What do you think the cartoonist's message is?
that the rich had too much power and money
when do i use affect vs effect

'Affect' is usually a VERB meaning to influence: 'The rain affected my mood.' 'Effect' is usually a NOUN meaning the result: 'The rain had an effect on my mood.' Remember:
  • Affect = Action (both start with A)
  • Effect = End result (both start with E)
There are rare exceptions, but this covers 95% of cases. Clear?
the A for action thing helps a lot
how do i write a dbq essay

A DBQ (Document-Based Question) essay requires you to analyze provided documents and use outside knowledge. Structure:
  • Introduction with thesis
  • Body paragraphs that group documents by theme
  • Analysis of each document's point of view/purpose/context
  • Outside evidence
What part are you struggling with?
analyzing the documents point of view
what is verbal irony
i dont get colon vs semicolon

A colon (:) introduces or explains - it says 'here's what I mean' or introduces a list. A semicolon (;) connects two related independent clauses - it's like a soft period.

Example with colon: 'I need three things: eggs, milk, bread.'
Example with semicolon: 'I love pizza; it's my favorite food.'

See the difference?
so colons are like presenting something and semicolons connect ideas
can you help me analyze the ending of the stranger by camus

Sure. At the end of The Stranger, Meursault embraces what Camus calls the absurd: the world doesn't provide meaning, so he stops pretending it does. His "peace" comes from dropping false hope and facing reality directly.

Which part confuses you most: the chaplain scene, his anger, or the last paragraph?
the last paragraph, like "the gentle indifference of the world"
i need an interpretive sentence about imagery in the things they carried

An interpretive sentence does two jobs: it names a device and explains what it reveals about a theme. Template:

Through [specific image], O'Brien suggests that [interpretation], highlighting [theme].

What image/scene are you focusing on (a quote helps)?
the list of things they carry at the start
i keep missing main idea questions on act reading

For ACT Reading main idea questions, think: "If I had to title this passage in 6 words, what would it be?" Then check which answer matches the whole passage (not one paragraph). Fast method:
  • Read first + last paragraph carefully
  • Skim topic sentences in the middle
  • Cross out choices that are too narrow or too broad
Are you running out of time, or just picking traps?
mostly time, i read too slowly
how do i structure the act writing essay

Use a simple 4-paragraph structure that scorers reward:
  • Intro: take a clear position + preview 2 reasons
  • Body 1: reason 1 + example
  • Body 2: reason 2 + example
  • Counterclaim: acknowledge + refute, then conclude
What prompt are you practicing (even a rough topic)?
prompt is about whether schools should start later in the morning
in ap lang rhetorical analysis, i can summarize but i dont know what to say about choices

In rhetorical analysis, avoid "what" (summary) and write "how + why." A good sentence frame is:

The author uses [choice] to [do what to the audience], which advances the purpose of [purpose] because [why it works].

Common choices: diction, syntax, imagery, tone shifts, comparisons, concessions. What passage/speaker are you analyzing?
a speech about climate action
in ap lang synthesis, how do i use sources without just summarizing them

Think of sources as evidence, not the essay itself. Do this loop:
  • Make a claim in your voice
  • Drop a specific detail from a source
  • Explain how it proves your claim
  • Connect it to the bigger argument
Also, pair sources ("Source A supports..., but Source C complicates...") to show synthesis. What topic is your prompt on?
it's about whether cities should ban single-use plastics
in ap lang argument, help me build a line of reasoning

A line of reasoning is a chain: thesis → reasons → evidence → warrant (why it matters). Try this structure:
  • Thesis with a qualifier ("generally," "in most cases")
  • Reason 1 (principle)
  • Reason 2 (consequence)
  • Counterclaim + rebuttal
Pick a topic and stance (even something simple like "school uniforms" or "social media").
i think school uniforms should not be required
on act english, which sentence correctly uses a colon

A colon works when the left side is a complete sentence and the right side explains or lists. Quick check: if you can replace the colon with "namely," it's probably correct.

Send me the answer choices and I'll help you eliminate them.

choices are: A) "My favorite fruits are: apples, bananas, and grapes." B) "I have three favorite fruits: apples, bananas, and grapes." C) "My favorite fruits are apples, bananas, and grapes." D) "My favorite fruits: apples, bananas, and grapes, are cheap."
por vs para is confusing (spanish)

Quick rule: para points forward (goal/destination), por explains why/how (reason/exchange).
  • Para: purpose (para estudiar), recipient (para mi madre), deadline (para el lunes)
  • Por: cause (por eso), duration (por dos horas), exchange (por cinco dólares), "thanks" (gracias por...)
Want to try: how would you say "Thanks for your help"?
gracias para tu ayuda? or por?
passe compose vs imparfait is confusing (french)

Think of a timeline: imparfait = background/ongoing, passé composé = completed event.

If time is a line, imparfait is like shading the background, and passé composé is like a dot: $\text{background} \;\longrightarrow\;$ then $\bullet$ something happens.
  • Imparfait: habits, descriptions, ongoing states (je pensais, il faisait froid)
  • Passé composé: specific actions, beginnings/endings (j'ai décidé, elle est arrivée)
Try this: "When I was little, I played outside." Which tense goes with "was little"?
imparfait? like "quand j'etais petit"
how do i write a thesis for a literary analysis essay

A strong literary thesis names what (claim about meaning) + how (techniques) + why (theme/insight). Template:

In [work], [author] uses [technique 1] and [technique 2] to reveal [complex claim], suggesting that [bigger idea].

What book/poem are you writing about?
the great gatsby
in us history, what caused the mexican american war

Major causes included:
  • Annexation of Texas (1845) and a border dispute (Rio Grande vs Nueces River)
  • Manifest Destiny and U.S. desire for western land/ports
  • Polk's expansion goals (California and New Mexico)
Mexico viewed U.S. actions as aggressive and illegitimate. Do you need this for a short answer or a longer essay?
short answer, and my teacher keeps mentioning polk
how did the new deal change the role of government

The New Deal expanded the federal government's role by creating programs that directly affected daily life:
  • Relief: immediate aid (CCC, WPA)
  • Recovery: restart the economy (NRA, agricultural supports)
  • Reform: long-term rules (Social Security, SEC, banking reforms)
It set the expectation that the government should help manage the economy during crises. Are you supposed to include a specific example program?
yeah, also what was the supreme court issue
what is federalism in simple terms

Federalism is sharing power between a national government and state governments. Some powers are federal (like declaring war), some are state (like running local schools), and some are shared (like collecting taxes).

Want examples of each category for a civics quiz?
yes please, like one federal power and one state power and one shared power
what was the scramble for africa

The Scramble for Africa (late 1800s) was the rapid colonization of African territories by European powers. Motivations are often summarized as "3 G's":
  • Gold (resources/markets)
  • Glory (national prestige)
  • God (missionary/"civilizing" claims)
It led to artificial borders, exploitation, and long-term conflict. Have you learned about the Berlin Conference yet?
yeah what was the point of that conference
why did ww2 start in europe

A big chain of causes: Treaty of Versailles resentment + economic crisis + rise of fascism + appeasement. The immediate trigger was Germany invading Poland on Sept. 1, 1939, after the Nazi-Soviet Pact reduced Hitler's fear of a two-front war. What part do you need to explain: Versailles, appeasement, or Hitler's goals?
appeasement, especially the munich agreement
what was the silk road and why did it matter

The Silk Road was a network of trade routes connecting China, Central Asia, the Middle East, and Europe. It mattered because it moved more than goods:
  • Products: silk, spices, textiles
  • Ideas: Buddhism, Islam, technologies
  • Disease: the Black Death spread along trade networks
Do you need an example of cultural diffusion for a paragraph?
yeah, cultural diffusion example please
what is plato's allegory of the cave about

It's a story about the difference between appearance and reality. Prisoners only see shadows on a wall, so they mistake shadows for truth. When one escapes, he realizes the outside world is more real, but returning to tell others is painful because they resist change.

What do you think the "shadows" represent in real life?
maybe the shadows are like misinformation and people only seeing what theyre told
what is the difference between kant and utilitarianism

Utilitarianism judges actions by outcomes (maximize happiness). Kant judges actions by duty and principle (follow moral rules you could apply universally).

Example: if lying would help someone, utilitarianism might allow it; Kant generally says lying is wrong because it can't be a universal rule. Want to try a practice scenario?
yeah like lying to protect a friend
what is baroque art

Baroque (1600s) is known for drama and emotion: intense movement, strong contrast, and theatrical lighting. It often aims to make viewers feel something immediately.

Key features:
  • Chiaroscuro (light/dark contrast)
  • Dynamic composition (diagonals, motion)
  • Realism + intensity
Are you looking at Caravaggio, Bernini, or someone else?
caravaggio, like the calling of saint matthew
dramatic irony in romeo and juliet examples?

Dramatic irony is when the audience knows something characters don't. In Romeo and Juliet:
  • We know Juliet isn't dead; Romeo thinks she is.
  • Juliet doesn't know Romeo is at her tomb.
  • Romeo doesn't know the Friar's plan fully worked.
Which scene are you writing about (balcony, Tybalt, tomb)?
the tomb scene
analyze ozymandias by shelley

Ozymandias uses a ruined statue to show that power is temporary. The irony is that the king's boast survives, but only to highlight his collapse. Notice the contrast between:
  • "king of kings" (arrogance)
  • "lone and level sands" (emptiness/time)
Do you need theme, tone, or specific literary devices for your assignment?
tone and devices
on act english, how do i fix run ons fast

If you see two independent clauses, you need one of these fixes:
  • Period: Sentence. Sentence.
  • Semicolon: Sentence; sentence.
  • Comma + conjunction: Sentence, and sentence.
  • Subordination: Because/although..., sentence.
Trap: a comma alone is a comma splice. Want to try a sample sentence?
yeah: "I studied all night, I still forgot the formulas."
help me write a hook for an essay about social media

A good hook is specific, not generic. Options that work:
  • Micro-scene: a 2-sentence moment
  • Surprising stat (if you can cite it)
  • Paradox: "more connected, more alone"
What's your thesis direction: harms, benefits, or a balanced argument?
balanced, like it helps activism but hurts attention
for a sentence combining question, how do i choose the best revision

Pick the option that keeps meaning and improves style. Quick checklist:
  • No new grammar errors
  • No redundancy
  • Clear logical relationship (cause/contrast)
  • Most concise without sounding choppy
Send the original two sentences + the answer choices.

original: "The museum expanded in 2010. It added a new wing for modern art." choices: A) "The museum expanded in 2010, it added a new wing for modern art." B) "The museum expanded in 2010 and added a new wing for modern art." C) "The museum expanded in 2010; and it added a new wing for modern art." D) "Expanding in 2010, a new wing for modern art was added by the museum."
on act reading paired passages, how do i answer "author 1 would respond" questions

Do it like a debate. Step 1: write a 6-word "claim" for each author. Step 2: label their tone (optimistic, skeptical, cautious). Step 3: when asked how Author 1 would respond to Author 2, look for the choice that matches Author 1's claim and tone.

Do you usually mix up who believes what, or is it the wording of the choices?
i mix up who believes what
what are the differences between hamilton and jefferson (apush)

A quick comparison:
  • Hamilton: strong federal government, national bank, industrial/commercial economy, loose interpretation of Constitution
  • Jefferson: stronger state power, agrarian ideal, strict interpretation, fear of centralized tyranny
For a short response, add one policy example (National Bank debate, Whiskey Rebellion, etc.). Do you need a paragraph or a chart?
a short paragraph please
why is the 14th amendment important

The 14th Amendment (1868) is huge because it defines citizenship and expands civil rights protections:
  • Birthright citizenship
  • Due process protections
  • Equal protection under the law
Later, courts used it to apply parts of the Bill of Rights to states ("incorporation"). Are you connecting it to Reconstruction or to modern cases?
mostly reconstruction, but our teacher mentioned brown v board too
what was the great migration

The Great Migration (roughly 1916-1970) was when millions of African Americans moved from the rural South to Northern and Western cities. Push/pull factors included:
  • Push: Jim Crow, violence, limited opportunities
  • Pull: factory jobs (especially during WWI/WWII), greater political/social possibilities
Do you need effects on culture (like the Harlem Renaissance) or on politics/labor?
culture please, like the harlem renaissance connection
in world history, what is nationalism in the 1800s

Nationalism is the belief that people who share language/culture/history should have political unity and self-rule. In the 1800s it fueled:
  • Unification (Italy, Germany)
  • Independence movements (in empires like Austria-Hungary/Ottoman)
  • Rivalries that contributed to WWI
Are you learning this through the Congress of Vienna / revolutions unit?
yeah congress of vienna and the revolutions unit
in the french revolution, what was the reign of terror

The Reign of Terror (1793-1794) was a period when revolutionary leaders (especially Robespierre and the Committee of Public Safety) used extreme measures—trials and executions—to "protect" the revolution from enemies. Thousands were executed, often by guillotine.

Do you need causes (war/fear), key figures, or consequences (backlash/thermidorian reaction)?
consequences, like what happens after robespierre

what is an unreliable narrator

An unreliable narrator is a storyteller whose account can't be fully trusted—because of bias, limited knowledge, trauma, deception, or misunderstanding. Authors use it to create suspense and force readers to interpret clues.

Common signs:
  • Contradictions
  • Other characters disagree
  • Overly defensive tone
  • Details that don't add up

what is the mandate of heaven
